contamination.brief_line: 方向：这篇讲在象岛上定下的一个求援决策：为什么把目标定在八百英里外的南乔治亚而不是更近的福克兰，谁去谁留、带什么丢什么、走之前怎么交代留守的人 (SOUTH-EL1-E4)(SOUTH-EL1-E7)(SOUTH-EL1-E13)(SOUTH-EL1-E17)。看点是把一个胜算很小的选项对全队讲清楚、让人自愿跟从，并且愿意承担拒绝病号上船的代价 (SOUTH-EL1-E6)(SOUTH-EL1-E10)(SOUTH-EL1-E12)。不要写成英雄赞歌，不要用“他当然会成功”的口吻，也不要把拒绝病号上船写成一句冷酷或高尚的道德判断 (SOUTH-EL1-E12)。
- 粮食只够全队按足额吃五个星期，减量可撑三个月，海兽可能不来，于是定为每天一顿热食 (SOUTH-EL1-E2)。
- 几名队员的健康和精神状况令人担心，一名队员双脚冻伤、医生说不动手术就保不住脚趾 (SOUTH-EL1-E1)。
- 判断必须有人乘船出海求援，而且不能拖 (SOUTH-EL1-E3)。
- 福克兰的斯坦利港更近，但要顶着常年西北风用一条脆弱的小船抢风航行；南乔治亚八百英里外，但在西风带内，东岸各捕鲸站可能找到人，冰情允许的话一个月可望往返 (SOUTH-EL1-E4)。
- 算过最坏情形：岛上的人风险不会因此增加，冬天少六张嘴，船上只带六人一个月的口粮；而象岛不会有任何人来搜寻他们 (SOUTH-EL1-E5)。
- 向全队讲清利害：五月中合恩角以南是世界上最暴虐的水域，出海只为援助的急迫需要 (SOUTH-EL1-E6)。
- Worsley 和 Wild 都要求同行；指定 Wild 留守全队，并交代万一求援失败，春季带人去 Deception Island (SOUTH-EL1-E7)。
- 选 Worsley 随行，理由是他定位快而准，尤其在困难情况下 (SOUTH-EL1-E8)。
- 征求志愿者，但作者写明心里其实已有名单 (SOUTH-EL1-E9)。
- Crean 原本要留下当 Wild 的帮手，他恳求上船，与 Wild 商量后带上他 (SOUTH-EL1-E10)。
- 有人不够强壮，有人不是熟练水手，虽然近几个月的经历也算得一点水手资格 (SOUTH-EL1-E11)。
- 有人提议带上病号让他尽快得到温暖和庇护，被否掉：健康的人在船上都难活，重病躺舱底的人熬不过必定遇到的坏天气 (SOUTH-EL1-E12)。
- 最后定下 Worsley、Crean、McNeish、McCarthy、Vincent 和作者六人 (SOUTH-EL1-E13)。
- 木匠年过五十、身体不算好，但懂帆船、手快 (SOUTH-EL1-E14)。
- 他把另一条船的桅杆横放作龙骨加强，用箱盖和雪橇板搭骨架，冻硬的帆布在油炉上一寸寸烤开再缝成覆罩；覆罩看着像舞台布景，但事后证明确实顶用 (SOUTH-EL1-E15)。
- 看到浮冰随时可能合拢，决定次日出发；在象岛的最后一夜又冷又不舒服 (SOUTH-EL1-E16)。
- 上岸交代留守的 Wild，写明几乎把整个局面和行动范围都交给他自行判断，并当面说信任他、把队伍托付给他 (SOUTH-EL1-E17)。
- 启航时留在岸上的人挥手欢呼 (SOUTH-EL1-E18)。
- 船上做饭要三个人：一人护灯、两人护锅 (SOUTH-EL1-E19)。
- 出海第六天船因结冰失去弹性，扔掉备用桨和两条湿透冻硬的睡袋，剩下四条，其中一条留给有人彻底垮掉时应急 (SOUTH-EL1-E20)。
- 缆绳断、海锚丢失，只能在大风里升帆顶风 (SOUTH-EL1-E21)。
- 出海第七天见太阳，观测显示已走三百八十多英里，接近南乔治亚的一半 (SOUTH-EL1-E22)。
- 第十一天夜里遇到前所未见的巨浪，船被抛起又挣脱出来 (SOUTH-EL1-E23)。
- Vincent 一周来已不再承担船员工作，作者写明无法解释他的垮掉：他身体本来是船上最强的 (SOUTH-EL1-E24)。
- 水要减到每人每天半品脱，有人恳求预支第二天的水被拒绝，因为风向一变航程会拖长 (SOUTH-EL1-E25)。

必须写明的不确定性：这套记录只有当事人一个史源，是他事后的第一人称自述 (SOUTH-EL1-E3)。文中的对话，例如把队伍托付给 Wild 的那句交代，是记述性的，未必逐字 (SOUTH-EL1-E17)；Crean 恳求随行也是同样情况 (SOUTH-EL1-E10)。不要替人物写心理：作者说看队员时“信心增加”只是自述，不是当时可核实的心理记录 (SOUTH-EL1-E13)；Vincent 为何垮掉作者自己说无法解释 (SOUTH-EL1-E24)。原文按出海后的天数记事，没有公元年份，文章里只用原文的天数与月份，不做换算 (SOUTH-EL1-E20)(SOUTH-EL1-E22)(SOUTH-EL1-E23)。距离、口粮、水的数字都照原文写，如两个距离、走了三百八十多英里、半品脱 (SOUTH-EL1-E4)(SOUTH-EL1-E5)(SOUTH-EL1-E22)(SOUTH-EL1-E25)。原文为扫描识别文本，个别字词有讹误，引用时照原文写法。

现代应用：资源有限、外部不会主动来救的小团队，要不要派人冒险出去求援、派谁去、谁留下看家、物资砍到什么程度、什么时候必须定下出发时点 (SOUTH-EL1-E2)(SOUTH-EL1-E3)(SOUTH-EL1-E5)(SOUTH-EL1-E13)(SOUTH-EL1-E16)；以及负责人临走前如何把决定权和责任一起交出去，说清楚失败时的后手 (SOUTH-EL1-E7)(SOUTH-EL1-E17)。

finally selected McNeish, McCarthy, and Vincent in addition to Worsley and Crean

edits.before: 这份记述出自《南方》作者欧内斯特·沙克尔顿的第一人称自述，他是这支队伍的队长。经过一段乘船航程后，他和全队困在象岛：粮食有限，有人冻伤，而且象岛上根本不会有人来搜寻他们。口粮按足额只够全队吃五个星期。减量可以撑三个月，或许还能靠海豹和象海豹补一些，但沙克尔顿不敢把信心全押在这上面：海滩上的海兽似乎都走了，冬天近了。燃料主要靠海兽脂肪，存量里有三只海豹和两张半带脂肪的兽皮。初步估量形势后，他决定全队每天只吃一顿热食。
edits.after: 队长欧内斯特·沙克尔顿和他的队伍困在象岛上，最后六人乘一条小船出海求援，二十二人留在岛上。下面的经过出自他在《南方》中的第一人称自述。经过一段乘船航程后，他们粮食有限，有人冻伤，而且象岛上根本不会有人来搜寻他们。口粮按足额只够全队吃五个星期。减量可以撑三个月，或许还能靠海豹和象海豹补一些。但沙克尔顿不敢把信心全押在这上面：海滩上的海兽似乎都走了，冬天近了。燃料主要靠海兽脂肪。初步估量形势后，他决定全队每天只吃一顿热食。

edits.before: This account comes from the first-person narrative of Ernest Shackleton, author of South and leader of this party. After a boat journey, he and his men were stranded on Elephant Island: food was limited, a man was frostbitten, and there was no chance at all of any search being made for them there. At full ration the food would last the whole party five weeks. Cut back, it could be spread over three months, and would probably be supplemented to some extent by seals and sea-elephants — but Shackleton dared not count on that with full confidence. The animals seemed to have deserted the beach and winter was near. They were mainly dependent on blubber for fuel, and their stocks included three seals and two and a half skins with the blubber attached. After a preliminary survey of the situation, he decided the party must be limited to one hot meal a day.
edits.after: Ernest Shackleton, leader of the party, and his men were stranded on Elephant Island; in the end six sailed for help in one small boat and twenty-two stayed on the island. What follows comes from his first-person account in South. After a boat journey, their food was limited, a man was frostbitten, and there was no chance at all of any search being made for them there. At full ration the food would last the whole party five weeks. Cut back, it could be spread over three months, and would probably be supplemented to some extent by seals and sea-elephants. But Shackleton dared not count on that with full confidence: the animals seemed to have deserted the beach and winter was near. They were mainly dependent on blubber for fuel. After a preliminary survey of the situation, he decided the party must be limited to one hot meal a day.

edits.before: 航程中有一次，遇上了队长二十六年海上经历中从未见过的巨浪，与多日来那些白浪翻卷的大浪完全不同。他高喊大家抓紧。船被像软木塞一样抛起、向前甩出，灌进半船水，在重击下颤抖；所有人拼命用随手抓到的容器掏水，十分钟后才觉得船重新有了生命。文森特在过去一周已不再是积极的船员，队长写明难以解释他的垮掉——他是船上体格最强壮的人之一，年轻，在北海拖网船上干过，本该比麦卡锡更能吃苦，而麦卡锡没那么强壮，却总是乐呵呵的。淡水减到每人每天半品脱。带上船的冰块早已用完，装船时一只水桶在浪里被撞裂，渗进了一些海水，喝的水发咸，渴得更厉害；队长不肯增加配给，有人恳求预支第二天的水，也被拒绝：万一风向不利，船可能被吹离海岛，航程拖长许多天。原文感叹，缺水是人所能承受的最严酷的匮乏。5月8日中午12点30分，麦卡锡从云隙中望见南乔治亚的黑色悬崖，距离开象岛整十四天。但岩岸看似直落入海，夜色将近，天气征兆也不好，那时贸然登陆无异自杀，只能离岸停驶，等待天亮。次日清晨风向转为西北，迅速增强为他们所有人经历过的最猛的飓风之一，风浪把船推向海岸，他们无能为力。直到天黑后风向突然转变，他们才得以重新驶离海岸；大风刚缓，锁住桅杆的销钉就掉了出来——队长写道，飓风中它若脱落，谁也救不了他们。5月10日，他们驶向一处队长认为必定是哈康国王湾（King Haakon Bay）的大海湾；风向转为从湾内吹出，他们在强风中抢风五次，才穿过礁石进入宽阔的湾口。暮色将近，他们转向海湾南岸一处有礁石护着的小湾。小船乘着涌浪触到海滩，几分钟后众人都平安上了岸；他们在脚边发现一条淡水溪流，随即跪下大口痛饮。但上岸并不等于求援成功：冰川和陡峭的山坡挡住了从小湾进入内陆的路，他们还得驶向海湾顶端，而指望找到捕鲸人的捕鲸站在东岸。

edits.before: At one point came a wave beyond anything the leader had met in twenty-six years at sea — a mighty upheaval of the ocean, quite apart from the white-capped seas that had been their tireless enemies for many days. He shouted for everyone to hold on: "It's got us!" The boat was lifted and flung forward like a cork, half-full of water and shuddering under the blow; the men baled with the energy of men fighting for life, and after ten minutes of uncertainty felt her renew her life beneath them. Vincent had for the past week ceased to be an active member of the crew, and the leader could not easily account for his collapse: physically one of the strongest men in the boat, young, with service on North Sea trawlers, he should have borne hardship better than McCarthy, who was not so strong but always happy. The daily water allowance was cut to half a pint a man. The lumps of ice taken aboard were long gone, and the breaker had been slightly stove in during loading, letting in some sea-water, so the brackish water sharpened the thirst; the leader would not raise the allowance or let anyone draw against the morrow's, however he was begged — should the wind turn unfavourable, it might drive them away from the island and lengthen the voyage by many days. Lack of water, the account adds, is the severest privation men can be condemned to endure. At 12.30 p.m. on May 8, McCarthy caught a glimpse of the black cliffs of South Georgia through a rift in the clouds, just fourteen days after leaving Elephant Island. But the rocky coast seemed to drop sheer to the sea, night was drawing near and the weather signs were unfavourable; to have attempted a landing then would have been suicidal, so they hauled off and hove to, waiting for dawn. Early the next morning the wind shifted to the north-west and quickly rose to one of the worst hurricanes any of them had ever experienced; wind and sea were driving them ashore, and they could do nothing. Only after dark did the wind suddenly shift and leave them free to make an offing again; almost as soon as the gale eased, the pin that locked the mast to the thwart fell out — had it gone during the hurricane, the leader writes, nothing could have saved them. On May 10 they made for a big indentation the leader thought must be King Haakon Bay; with the wind blowing out of the bay, they tacked five times in the strong wind before getting through the reef into the wide mouth of the bay. With dusk approaching, they turned toward a small cove guarded by a reef on the south side of the bay. The boat ran in on a swell and touched the beach, and in a few minutes they were all safe ashore; finding a stream of fresh water almost at their feet, they were soon down on their knees drinking. But landing was not the same as securing relief: glaciers and precipitous mountain slopes barred the way inland from the cove, they still had to sail to the head of the sound, and the whaling stations where whalers could be counted on lay on the east coast.

edits.before: Read together, these decisions suggest one explanation: what made the plan speakable was the arithmetic of the worst case. The boat party carried a month's provisions; if they did not make South Georgia within the month, they were sure to go under. The men left behind would have fewer mouths to feed through the winter. The worst case was calculated as adding nothing to the risks of the men left on the island. According to the author's preface, the twenty-two men left on Elephant Island eked out a bare existence there for four and a half months, far beyond the hoped-for return with relief within a month; this piece draws no causal verdict from that. This piece infers that when every option is grim, people will follow not necessarily the more hopeful road, but the one that costs its losses honestly and does not shift them onto comrades.

edits.before: One more detail catches the eye: the account says he decided to call for volunteers while already having a pretty good idea of his choices. The original states that he called the men together, explained his plan and asked for volunteers, and that many came forward at once; yet the final selection was still his. One alternative this piece raises would have been simply to name names and skip the formality. One reading is that explaining the plan and arguing the dangers and reasons to the party in detail before asking for volunteers may make the list read as consensus rather than assignment. This is only one reading, and the passages quoted give no reason for the arrangement.

edits.before: This record rests on exactly one historical source: a first-person account written after the fact by one of those involved. The author says the account of the voyage to South Georgia is based on scanty notes made day by day, which usually dealt with the bare facts of distances, positions and weather, while the incidents themselves came from memory. Its dialogue is reported, not transcribed — the words entrusting the party to Wild, Crean's plea for a place in the boat — and need not be verbatim. The leader's statement that his confidence grew as he looked at the men is retrospective self-description, not a verifiable record of his state of mind at the time.

edits.before: 航程中有一次，遇上了队长二十六年海上经历中从未见过的巨浪，与多日来那些白浪翻卷的大浪完全不同。他高喊大家抓紧。船被像软木塞一样抛起、向前甩出，灌进半船水，在重击下颤抖；所有人拼命用随手抓到的容器掏水，十分钟后才觉得船重新有了生命。文森特在过去一周已不再是积极的船员，队长写明难以解释他的垮掉——他是船上体格最强壮的人之一，年轻，在北海拖网船上干过，本该比麦卡锡更能吃苦，而麦卡锡没那么强壮，却总是乐呵呵的。淡水减到每人每天半品脱。带上船的冰块早已用完，装船时一只水桶在浪里被撞裂，渗进了一些海水，喝的水发咸，渴得更厉害。队长不肯增加配给，因为万一风向不利，船可能被吹离海岛，航程拖长许多天；有人恳求预支第二天的水，他也坚决拒绝。原文感叹，缺水是人所能承受的最严酷的匮乏。5月8日中午12点30分，麦卡锡从云隙中望见南乔治亚的黑色悬崖，距离开象岛整十四天。但岩岸看似直落入海，夜色将近，天气征兆也不好，那时贸然登陆无异自杀，只能离岸停驶，等待天亮。次日清晨风向转为西北，迅速增强为他们所有人经历过的最猛的飓风之一，风浪把船推向海岸，他们无能为力。直到天黑后风向突然转变，他们才得以重新驶离海岸；大风刚缓，锁住桅杆的销钉就掉了出来——队长写道，飓风中它若脱落，谁也救不了他们。5月10日，他们驶向一处队长认为必定是哈康国王湾（King Haakon Bay）的大海湾；风向转为从湾内吹出，他们在强风中抢风五次，才穿过礁石进入宽阔的湾口。暮色将近，他们转向海湾南岸一处有礁石护着的小湾。小船乘着涌浪触到海滩，几分钟后众人都平安上了岸；他们在脚边发现一条淡水溪流，随即跪下大口痛饮。但上岸并不等于求援成功：冰川和陡峭的山坡挡住了从小湾进入内陆的路，他们还得驶向海湾顶端，而指望找到捕鲸人的捕鲸站在东岸。

edits.before: At one point came a wave beyond anything the leader had met in twenty-six years at sea — a mighty upheaval of the ocean, quite apart from the white-capped seas that had been their tireless enemies for many days. He shouted for everyone to hold on: "It's got us!" The boat was lifted and flung forward like a cork, half-full of water and shuddering under the blow; the men baled with the energy of men fighting for life, and after ten minutes of uncertainty felt her renew her life beneath them. Vincent had for the past week ceased to be an active member of the crew, and the leader could not easily account for his collapse: physically one of the strongest men in the boat, young, with service on North Sea trawlers, he should have borne hardship better than McCarthy, who was not so strong but always happy. The daily water allowance was cut to half a pint a man. The lumps of ice taken aboard were long gone, and the breaker had been slightly stove in during loading, letting in some sea-water, so the brackish water sharpened the thirst. The leader would not raise the allowance, since an unfavourable wind might drive them away from the island and lengthen the voyage by many days; when he was begged to let anyone draw against the morrow's allowance, he firmly refused. Lack of water, the account adds, is the severest privation men can be condemned to endure. At 12.30 p.m. on May 8, McCarthy caught a glimpse of the black cliffs of South Georgia through a rift in the clouds, just fourteen days after leaving Elephant Island. But the rocky coast seemed to drop sheer to the sea, night was drawing near and the weather signs were unfavourable; to have attempted a landing then would have been suicidal, so they hauled off and hove to, waiting for dawn. Early the next morning the wind shifted to the north-west and quickly rose to one of the worst hurricanes any of them had ever experienced; wind and sea were driving them ashore, and they could do nothing. Only after dark did the wind suddenly shift and leave them free to make an offing again; almost as soon as the gale eased, the pin that locked the mast to the thwart fell out — had it gone during the hurricane, the leader writes, nothing could have saved them. On May 10 they made for a big indentation the leader thought must be King Haakon Bay; with the wind blowing out of the bay, they tacked five times in the strong wind before getting through the reef into the wide mouth of the bay. With dusk approaching, they turned toward a small cove guarded by a reef on the south side of the bay. The boat ran in on a swell and touched the beach, and in a few minutes they were all safe ashore; finding a stream of fresh water almost at their feet, they were soon down on their knees drinking. But landing was not the same as securing relief: glaciers and precipitous mountain slopes barred the way inland from the cove, they still had to sail to the head of the sound, and the whaling stations where whalers could be counted on lay on the east coast.

issues.problem: 开头先讲史源（《南方》作者的第一人称自述），然后才讲处境；全文开头一直没有说明这支队伍有多少人、最后几人出海、几人留下，读者说不清“谁遇到了问题”。同时开头堆了读者此时还用不上的存量细节（三只海豹、两张半兽皮）。

evidence.quote: twenty-two of my comrades eked out a bare existence for four and a half months

issues.proposed: 开头先写处境：队长沙克尔顿和他的队伍困在象岛，最后六人乘小船出海求援，二十二人留在岛上。史源说明后移一句。“三只海豹和两张半带脂肪的兽皮”可以移到口粮那句之后或者压缩，但“燃料主要靠海兽脂肪”要保留。英文同步。

issues.problem: 把“风向不利可能拖长航程”写成既是不增加配给的理由，也是拒绝预支第二天的水的理由。证据只把这个理由用于不增加配给，拒绝预支另写一句，没有附理由。这个合并的写法与已知污染 K26 的简报说法一致。

issues.problem: 一段之内连续写了巨浪、文森特垮掉、限水、望见陆地、飓风、销钉、入湾、登陆、上岸后的处境，读者很难分清先后。
